abstract: In humans, hands are animate effectors and tools are visually dissimilar inanimate objects, yet the brain represents them in closely related cortical systems. Whether this coupling depends uniquely on human tool knowledge or reflects a conserved property of primate cortex is unknown. Using whole brain fMRI (0.22 cubic mm voxels) in macaques viewing images of hands, tools, and other objects, we found that inferotemporal cortex largely followed the animate/inanimate division, with only a few small hand-tool preferring sites. In contrast, parietal and prefrontal areas showed hand-tool representational similarities that were best matched by a neural-network model trained on fine-grained human hand-object interactions rather than by networks optimized for static object recognition or general action recognition. Volumetric functional ultrasound imaging (0.0023 cubic mm voxels) independently showed that tool responses were spatially aligned with human hand, but not monkey hand, responses in posterior parietal cortex. Macaque cortex thus represents tools in relation to the hand even without habitual tool use, consistent with an evolutionarily conserved action related scaffold that may be shaped by longterm visual exposure to human hand tool interactions.
